primary_claim: Slingshots (training-loss spikes with sudden weight-norm increases under AdamW) are explained, for hinge loss, by momentum decaying to zero in a flat loss basin followed by a weight-decay-driven exit; this explanation partially transfers to cross-entropy loss; and empirically, slingshots reduce test loss more than equivalent non-slingshot training intervals or random-direction jumps of the same magnitude, in 1-hidden-layer MLPs trained on k-sparse parity.

effect.metric: log ratio of test loss after vs. before interval
effect.value: median log ratio -0.438 (slingshot) vs -0.039 (no slingshot) vs -0.369 (random jump), across 100 training runs; slingshot vs no-slingshot difference significant (p<0.05, Mood's median test), slingshot vs random jump not significant (p>0.05)

contradicts_or_qualifies: Thilak et al.'s reported slingshot regimes under Adam / zero weight decay and extreme decay factors, which the authors could not empirically replicate and which don't fit their explanation
stated_future_work: Connecting generalization and the inductive biases of adaptive optimizer methods needs further study
limitations_stated: Scope is limited to a simple one-hidden-layer MLP trained on a synthetic algorithmic task
The hinge-loss explanation only partially transfers to cross-entropy loss
Unable to empirically replicate several slingshot regimes from Thilak et al. (e.g. Adam with zero weight decay, extreme decay factors)
The method for detecting slingshots (and thus the random-jump comparison) is somewhat unprincipled
No good explanation for why slingshots induce better generalization than random jumps
quote: empirical evidence that slingshots are biased towards decreasing test loss
